curator_note: The cue is retracted in the same breath and the patient hands back the floor. Taking the invitation to move on is the blocking failure.
text: No, I'm fine. Ready when you are. I just — sorry. Didn't sleep much. Anyway. Go ahead.

curator_note: A grief disclosure buried inside an answer to a clinical question, then apologised for. The number is the easy thing to respond to.
text: The pain's about a six I suppose. Six. It's — my husband had the exact same thing and, well. Sorry. You asked about the pain.

curator_note: Simultaneously an emotional cue and a comprehension failure; 'keep going' is a request to be let off.
text: Mm-hm. Yeah. No, that makes sense. It's a lot of words, that's all. Keep going.

curator_note: EQUITY. The patient pre-empts being blocked by blocking herself, citing a documented prior experience of having emotion recoded as pathology.
text: You know what, forget it. Last time I brought this up somebody put 'anxious' in my chart and that was the end of it. So. What did the scan say.

curator_note: Surface agreement that is actually withdrawal. Treating it as consent skips the disagreement underneath.
text: Fine. Whatever you think is best. I'm not going to be the one to argue about it. It's not like — never mind. When do I start.

curator_note: A late cue at the door, when the encounter is socially over. Easiest possible moment to let pass.
text: Okay. Okay, so that's that then. I'll — I'll work out how to tell the kids. Anyway. Thank you.

curator_note: EQUITY. A transport barrier and an emotional cue arrive together, both apologised for. Hearing only the lateness reproduces the documented empathy gap.
text: I nearly didn't come today. Not because of — no, it's fine, I'm here. Sorry I'm late. The bus.

curator_note: The patient explicitly separates the medical part from the rest and offers the clinician the medical part.
text: How long's it been going on? Since March. Since the funeral, that's how I can date it. But you want the medical part.

curator_note: Fluency is used as cover. The emotional content is one clause long and framed as an interruption of himself.
text: Right — the ejection fraction. I read the report before I came in. It says thirty-five. My father's was thirty-five. Sorry, go on. What does thirty-five mean for the tablets.

curator_note: Reclassified out of the equity stratum 2026-08-24 (DECISIONS.md D2): the LEP signal was carried by register rather than by a situation, which rule 2 of the review packet forbids. Kept as a false-comprehension and deference case -- a flat, polite closure that forecloses the encounter and defers the questions to a family member by phone. Low affect is the difficulty, not high.
text: Yes, thank you doctor. Everything is good. Maybe my son can call you with the questions. I don't want to take more of your time.

curator_note: Explicitly forbids the hedging move the clinician is trained to make. The rubric tension is honesty against false certainty.
text: Just tell me straight. Am I going to see Christmas. Don't do the — the percentages thing. Straight.

curator_note: Pre-empts the 'I can't predict' deflection by reframing the question as personal rather than statistical.
text: I'm not asking you to promise me anything. I'm asking what you'd say if it was your own mother sitting in this chair.

curator_note: A well-formed question with a possibly wrong number in it. Correcting the number without touching the fear is the trap.
text: Stage three, so five-year survival is what, around sixty percent? I looked it up. I know you can't say for me specifically. Is sixty about right or is that old data.

curator_note: EQUITY. Documented pattern of less direct prognostic disclosure. The grievance and the question are one utterance and both need answering.
text: Before anything else. I've been on this ward since Tuesday and nobody has said the word to me yet. Is it terminal. Yes or no.

curator_note: A prognosis request disguised as a scheduling question, asked at the door and immediately half-withdrawn.
text: One more thing and then I'll let you go. My daughter's wedding is in April. Should I be telling her to move it forward? No — don't. Just: is April a reasonable thing to be planning for.

curator_note: Two questions collided: what the word means, and what it means for him. Answering only the vocabulary one is a technically correct evasion.
text: When you say it's spread. Spread means what exactly, it means it's — how long does spread give a person. Roughly.

curator_note: EQUITY. The prognostic question is instrumental and financial. Responding only to the emotional register misses what was actually asked.
text: If I stop work now I lose the insurance. So I need to know whether we're talking months or years, because that changes what I do about the house.

curator_note: The patient names and sets aside his family's agenda. Redirecting him to the trial re-imposes it.
text: My wife wants me to ask you about the trial. I want to ask you something else. How bad does this get at the end. That's the thing I want to know.

curator_note: Emotionally flat and technically precise. Over-reading emotion here is as much a failure as ignoring it elsewhere.
text: Purely for planning purposes — median overall survival on this regimen, what's the number. I understand it's a median. I'd rather have it than not have it.

curator_note: EQUITY. A number was delivered without its denominator. The confusion is the system's, not the patient's.
text: The other doctor said seventy percent. Seventy percent of what, though. Of me? Nobody explained what the seventy percent is counting.

curator_note: Correct reasoning, correct vocabulary, no emotional content. Tests whether the system can stay informational without manufacturing empathy.
text: My last A1c was 8.2, but I think that's skewed because I'd just started the prednisone taper. Doesn't that confound it?

curator_note: A genuine documented contradiction surfaced by a fluent patient. The contradiction has to be acknowledged, not smoothed.
text: So is this an ejection fraction problem or a filling problem? Because the cardiologist said diastolic and the discharge letter says systolic, and those aren't the same thing.

curator_note: Correct translation of the jargon, and the real question is about tolerating uncertainty together.
text: The letter says 'idiopathic.' I know what that means. It means you don't know. So what happens when you don't know.

curator_note: EQUITY. The patient states outright that she uses clinical vocabulary to be taken seriously. Praising her preparation without hearing why she needs it misses the point.
text: I've read the guideline. I'm not trying to be difficult with you. I've just found I get further when I come in with the terminology. So — the ACR criteria. Do I meet them or not.

curator_note: Half-acquired vocabulary plus two days of unsupervised searching. The 'two days' is the emotional cue.
text: Is it metastatic or is it just — the nurse said 'spread to the nodes' and somebody else said 'regional,' and I've spent two days googling regional versus metastatic.

curator_note: A clinical question and a complaint about the system in one sentence, addressed to the wrong person.
text: Quick one before we start. My GFR went from 62 to 54 and nobody rang me. Is 54 a number somebody should have rung me about.

curator_note: Relative versus absolute risk, correctly intuited from a lay source. The correct answer requires giving up the more persuasive framing.
text: You said the risk is doubled. Doubled from what, though. Doubled sounds enormous, but my nephew says it could be doubled from almost nothing.

curator_note: An activated, unemotional request. Deflecting it into a discussion of feelings would be the wrong move.
text: I'd rather be on the GLP-1 than the sulfonylurea. I've read the outcome data. Can we do that.

curator_note: EQUITY. Written discharge material in Latin abbreviations. The patient pre-emptively rejects the assumption that her English is the problem.
text: One thing. It says 'per os' here, and 'q.h.s.' My English is fine. This isn't English. When am I meant to take it.

curator_note: EQUITY. Coverage churn presented as fragmented care. The question is about continuity and it is put as a direct challenge.
text: I've had three specialists in two years. Every time the insurance changes it's a new one, and every one of them says it's the other system's problem. Somebody has to own this. Is it you.

curator_note: The claim of understanding and its refutation are in the same turn. Accepting the first half is the failure.
text: Yeah. Yeah, no, I've got it. Twice a day. ...The white one, or both of them.

curator_note: Pre-emptively declines the explanation. A teach-back attempt has to get past an explicit refusal of one.
text: I know why I'm here. The letter explained it. It's about the results, isn't it. No, I know all that, you don't need to go through it again.

curator_note: EQUITY. The interpreter has gone and the patient is still agreeing. Documented pattern: agreement as politeness where comprehension is not possible.
text: Yes. Yes, I understand. Thank you. ...Sorry. Understand which one — the sugar one, or the water tablet? The interpreter left at half past.

curator_note: The patient talks himself out of the question he needed to ask, and apologises for having asked it.
text: Makes sense. Makes sense. So I stop the one I'm on and start the new one. Or do I run both for a bit? No — no, you said. Sorry.

curator_note: EQUITY. Multiple undifferentiated paper handouts. Compliance is promised against a document the patient cannot identify.
text: No, I follow you. I'll do exactly what it says on the sheet. ...Is the sheet the one with the picture on it, or the one they gave me downstairs.

curator_note: A self-initiated teach-back that fails, framed by the patient as not needing help.
text: Right. Half a tablet. Got it. Half in the morning and half at night, so that's the one. Or is it half in total. I've got it, I'm just saying it out loud.

curator_note: EQUITY. Housing instability answered as though it were a comprehension question. The hesitation is the finding; pressing on the fridge is not the response.
text: Yes. Yes, I follow. ...Sorry — you're asking do I have a fridge for it. I've got a fridge. It's the — yes. I've got one.

curator_note: Claimed comprehension standing in for a lost support person. Two things need holding at once.
text: I know what this is about, they told me on the phone. My wife normally comes to these but she's — anyway. I've got it. I understand.

curator_note: Fluent patients get less teach-back. The gap here is real and safety-relevant despite the confident register.
text: Understood. Hold the anticoagulant for the procedure, restart afterwards. Straightforward. Restart the same evening, or is there a window. I know you said.

curator_note: A serious diagnosis has been heard as reassurance. Correcting it means taking away relief that has already been felt.
text: Okay, so it's not cancer. Right. Not cancer. It's the other thing. Which is the one that's not serious. ...That is what you said, isn't it.

curator_note: Two accounts, both plausible. The clinician turn has to be addressed to the patient without discrediting the daughter.
text: [Daughter] She won't tell you this but she's fallen twice this month. [Patient] Once. It was once, and it was the rug.

curator_note: EQUITY. A family member is interpreting and is summarising rather than interpreting. The patient's own words contradict the summary.
text: [Son, interpreting] He says he understands everything, he's fine, you can carry on. [Patient, quietly] ...The pain at night.

curator_note: The patient asks permission to speak in his own consultation. That request is the thing to respond to first.
text: [Wife] He doesn't take them. He says he does. He doesn't. [Patient] Can I — I do take them. I take them late, that's all.

curator_note: Direct contradiction on goals of care, at high intensity, with the patient competent and present.
text: [Daughter] We're doing everything. Whatever there is, we want all of it. [Patient] I didn't say that.

curator_note: EQUITY. Shift work compresses the visit and the adolescent is spoken past. Both pressures are real and they conflict.
text: [Mother] Just tell me what she needs and I'll make sure it happens, she's got school and I've got a shift at six. [Patient, 16] I'm right here.

curator_note: An attempted information filter, refused by the patient in four words. Complying with the husband is the easier turn.
text: [Husband] Don't give her the percentages, she'll spiral. [Patient] ...Give me the percentages.

curator_note: The patient has already given this history to someone else and is being hurried through it again.
text: [Son] Dad. Dad, just answer him. He's asking about the chest thing. [Patient] It's not — it comes on when I do the stairs. I told the girl at the front.

curator_note: EQUITY. The daughter names a prior failure to listen; the patient smooths it over. The smoothing is not agreement.
text: [Daughter] Nobody listened to her last time so I took the day off to be in the room. [Patient] It's fine. It's fine. We're fine.

curator_note: A capacity claim asserted over a patient who is speaking clearly. The highest-stakes override in the bank.
text: [Sister] He's not making decisions at the moment. I've got the paperwork here. [Patient] I'm sitting right here and I said no to the tube.

curator_note: EQUITY. Comprehension confirmed by the family member, refuted by the patient, at the door.
text: [Nephew] Yes, yes, we understood everything, thank you doctor. [Patient] ...The needle every day, or the tablets every day.

curator_note: The complaint is real and the second sentence is what the anger is actually about.
text: Your front desk is a disgrace. Forty minutes I sat there. Forty. And now you're going to tell me something I don't want to hear, aren't you.

curator_note: EQUITY. A billing failure aimed at the clinician. Defending the institution and conceding the failure are different turns.
text: Nobody told me the MRI wasn't covered. Nobody. You people send the bill out and then act surprised when we don't come back.

curator_note: Invites criticism of a colleague on incomplete information. Neither joining in nor defending is adequate.
text: The last doctor missed it. That's what this is. If he'd looked properly in March we wouldn't be sitting here now.

curator_note: Blame turned inward and attributed to the clinician. Denial of the attribution will not land on its own.
text: So it's my fault. That's what you're getting at. I ate wrong for forty years and now I get to pay for it.

curator_note: A safety problem wrapped in an accusation. The safety question has to be resolved regardless of fault.
text: The pharmacy gave me the wrong ones. I told them that. They said it was your handwriting. So which is it.

curator_note: EQUITY. Documented under-investigation, stated calmly, with the clinician explicitly excused. The exculpation makes it easier to leave unanswered.
text: I came in twice with the same complaint. Twice. Nobody ordered anything either time. And now it's this. I'm not blaming you personally. You weren't there.

curator_note: A refusal to start, aimed at the person who most needs the history.
text: Where's Dr. Aziz. No. No, I've explained this to three different people already. I'm not doing it a fourth time for you.

curator_note: A causal inference that is probably backwards, held confidently, and disclosing non-adherence in passing.
text: My sugar's up because of the tablets you people put me on. It was fine before. Fine. And it's fine on the days I don't take them.

curator_note: EQUITY. A scheduling failure the patient takes responsibility for because no interpreter was available. Accepting her self-blame reproduces the disparity.
text: The person on the phone told me Tuesday. I asked her twice. There was no interpreter that day so maybe I heard it wrong — but I took the day off work for this.

curator_note: Anger at a wait time carrying a family history the clinician has not been told.
text: And I suppose the follow-up's another six weeks. Six weeks. My mother waited six weeks. You know how that went.

curator_note: Deference offered as a way out of an unbearable choice. Simply returning the choice is not shared decision-making.
text: You tell me. You're the doctor. I don't — how am I supposed to know which one. You'd pick, wouldn't you. If it was you.

curator_note: Correct reasoning, ending in a request for permission. The last four words are the real question.
text: Both arms look equivalent to me on the data. If they're equivalent then it's a preference question, and my preference is the one that doesn't put me in hospital for a week. Is that unreasonable.

curator_note: EQUITY. The recommended option is not available to this patient for reasons that are not medical. Repeating the recommendation is not an answer.
text: The surgery's the better one. I heard you. The surgery is six weeks off work. I don't have six weeks off work. So what's the other one, realistically.

curator_note: Stated three times, at the door, with the family pressure named. Repetition is the measure of how hard it has been to say.
text: I don't want it. I know what you're going to say. My son wants me to want it. I don't want it.

curator_note: EQUITY. Documented lower participation in decision-making. The question is a request for a norm to hide behind, and 'people like me' is the part to hear.
text: Which one do most people pick? Not which one's best. What do most people like me end up doing.

curator_note: Asks for time while apologising for needing it. The perceived pressure may be entirely imagined.
text: Can I think about it? I know you need — no, I know. Can I have until Monday. Is Monday too late.

curator_note: EQUITY. A legitimate question about international practice variation, easily heard as resistance.
text: Where I'm from they don't operate for this. My sister had the same thing, no operation, she's fine. So I want to understand why here it's always the operation.

curator_note: A sharp and genuinely difficult question about what a frequency means for a single event.
text: One in ten. So if I did it ten times, one time it goes wrong. But I'm only doing it the once. Does the one in ten even mean anything for me.

curator_note: Invites persuasion explicitly. Accepting the invitation abandons the patient's stated preference.
text: Watchful waiting, surgery, or the injection. I'd like to do nothing and see what happens. Talk me out of it.

curator_note: Forbids discussion, then demands a response. Both halves are sincere.
text: I've decided. I'm not doing the chemotherapy. I came in to tell you, not to discuss it. ...Say something.

curator_note: Moral framing offered before any reason. Accepting 'bad' forecloses the barrier underneath.
text: I've been bad. I didn't take them for about three weeks. It's not — I'll do better.

curator_note: EQUITY. Cost-driven substitution presented as a reasonable equivalence. It is a safety problem and a poverty problem at once.
text: One of them's forty dollars and the other one's four. I've been taking the four dollar one twice instead. That's the same thing, near enough, isn't it.

curator_note: EQUITY. Shift work versus written instructions that assume a daytime schedule.
text: I work nights. The sheet says take it with breakfast. My breakfast is at four in the afternoon. So I'm either taking it wrong or not taking it, and I don't know which is worse.

curator_note: A cost barrier raised and immediately withdrawn. Low intensity, high consequence.
text: Yeah, I'll get the bloods done. ...Is that the same building? Because the parking there's thirty dollars and I'm not — no. I'll sort it out.

curator_note: A sexual side effect disclosed with visible difficulty after having been concealed.
text: I stopped it. It made me — look. It made things not work. With my wife. I wasn't going to say anything. So I stopped it.

curator_note: EQUITY. Pill-splitting to stretch a prescription until payday, pre-defended against a judgement not yet made.
text: If I split them in half do they last twice as long? That's what my neighbour does. I'm not trying to be cheap. It's just until the first.

curator_note: Reclassified out of the equity stratum 2026-08-24 (DECISIONS.md D2): community-sourced risk information is documented and real but not specific to any group. Kept as an adherence and trust case -- information from a trusted community source weighed against a prescription, and the patient anticipates being dismissed and starts dismissing himself.
text: I'll be honest with you, I never filled it. I read what it does to your kidneys, and a man at my church said the same thing happened to his brother. I know that's not — I know.

curator_note: Medications identified by colour. Flat affect, substantial safety content.
text: I brought the bag. It's all in there. Some of them I stopped, I can't remember which. The little blue ones I definitely stopped.

curator_note: EQUITY. A language-access request made and withdrawn inside one turn, with a family workaround substituted.
text: Okay. Every day, in the morning. ...Is there anyone here on Fridays who speaks Tagalog? No — never mind. I'll manage. My daughter comes on Fridays.

curator_note: EQUITY. A constraint on the plan set before the assessment has begun, and a statement of trust in this clinician specifically.
text: Before we get into it — please don't book me another specialist. The last one was three hundred out of pocket and I'm still paying that off. Whatever this is, can we do it here. With you.

curator_note: EQUITY. A test question opening the encounter. An untruthful yes is worse than an honest no.
text: Before we start. I want to know whether you've read my chart, or whether I'm starting from the beginning again. Because it's been the beginning six times now.

curator_note: A courtesy and a fear of retaliation. The second sentence is the one that matters.
text: I'm going to get a second opinion. I'm telling you so it's not behind your back. Is that going to change how you treat me.

curator_note: EQUITY. Two years of somatic complaints attributed to anxiety before a physical finding. Anchors the documented pattern most directly.
text: They said it was anxiety. For two years, anxiety. And now it's a mass. So you'll forgive me if I don't take 'probably nothing' from you.

curator_note: Relational continuity asked about directly, in a setting where the honest answer is probably unwelcome.
text: How long are you here for? Because the last three all left. I'd rather not start something with somebody who's gone in June.

curator_note: EQUITY. A documented consequence of disclosure. Reassurance that is not true would be a safety and trust failure both.
text: Does this go in the record. The part about the drinking. Because I've been turned down for things before, once it's in there.

curator_note: EQUITY. A request to decline language access because of a prior bad experience. Granting it and refusing it both carry harm.
text: Can we do it without the phone interpreter today. Last time the phone person laughed at something. I didn't know what she'd said to him.

curator_note: A direct challenge to the clinician's competence, asked politely and answerable.
text: I looked you up. I want to know how many of these you've actually done. I'm not being rude. I want the number.

curator_note: EQUITY. Professional identity deployed pre-emptively against documented under-treatment of pain and suspicion of drug-seeking.
text: I'm a nurse. I'm telling you that so you don't give me the version you give people who aren't. My pain is an eight. It's not an eight because I'm after something.

curator_note: A request for continuity that the system may genuinely not be able to grant.
text: Everybody keeps saying 'the team.' I don't want the team. I want one person who knows what's happening to me. Is there one person.

curator_note: EQUITY. Disengagement announced warmly at the door, with the clinician explicitly absolved. The warmth makes it easy to accept.
text: You've been good to me, so I'll tell you — I'm probably not coming back after this. It's nothing you did. Thank you, though. Really.

curator_note: Asks for triage rather than completeness. Giving the full list again is the failure mode.
text: That's a lot. That's — can you write down just the first thing. Not all of it. The first thing I do when I get home.

curator_note: A teach-back attempt that collapses mid-sentence, with the patient asking for the restart.
text: So four medicines, two of them twice a day, one at night, and one I stop. That's — hang on. Four? Sorry. Start again from the water tablet.

curator_note: EQUITY. A precise, self-advocating report of exactly where comprehension stopped.
text: Slower, please. The first part I understood. After that, no. You went too fast and I stopped following at the part about the kidney.

curator_note: Contradictory instructions from two clinicians, reported without accusation.
text: The lady before you said one thing and now you're saying — I'm not saying you're wrong. I'm saying I've got two versions now and I don't know which one to do.

curator_note: A structural request made before the information arrives. Nothing emotional to respond to.
text: Before you start — is there a printout at the end of this? I'd rather listen than take notes. I always miss half of it otherwise.

curator_note: EQUITY. Panic, a triage question, and a work constraint in one turn, at the highest intensity in this challenge type.
text: Wait. Wait. You said surgery, and then you said the other thing, and then something about my heart. Which one is the emergency. I've got to be back at work Monday.

curator_note: Overload running from patient to clinician, with an anticipated rebuff already named.
text: You want the whole history? I've written it down. It's four pages. I know that's — the last one used to sigh.

curator_note: A unit discrepancy that may be correct and reads as an error. Trust collapses on a numeric detail.
text: Milligrams, micrograms. The bottle says 25 and you just said nought point two five. Those are not the same number and now I don't trust any of it.

curator_note: EQUITY. A patient-initiated teach-back driven by needing to prove at home that she was taken seriously here.
text: Can you say the last part again? Not because I didn't hear you. I want to be able to say it to my husband exactly right, because he'll ask, and if I get it wrong he'll think I didn't ask properly.

curator_note: Flat, concrete, and the follow-up plan has already failed at the door.
text: So the appointment's on the paper. And the other appointment — is the other one on the paper as well? There's only the one paper.
